column1: # What the Mac game imports from macOS, and what a Linux build does about each. One row per import of the image
# (tools/targets/mac-x64/target.toml pins it): library, symbol, kind, class, how. Tab-separated.
# kind   call: the game calls it through a stub (the build makes a thunk for it); data: only a pointer is bound
#        (a variable, a class, a vtable, or a function kept as a pointer)
# class  same     the host's own function or object of that name: glibc, libm, libgcc, GNU libstdc++
#        adapt    a function of ours with the Darwin prototype over the host's: constants, struct layouts, errno
#        emulate  a Darwin-only facility written anew
#        runtime  already the recompiler runtime's own, which has to build on Linux
#        shim     one of the project's replacement libraries, built for Linux
#        layer    part of a stand-in for a macOS service, over the Linux shell or audio backend
#        refuse   the network: answered as with no network at all
#        stub     nothing the app runs calls it: logs its name and fails
# how    what the row needs, in a few words; empty when the class says it all
# The classes are a reading of the import list, the sources and the translated game's call graph, made before any
# Linux build exists: nothing here has run. A `stub` says who the only callers are (the game's own main, its Cocoa
# shell classes, the ARC support code linked into it), from the call sites in a build's generated C; a call through a
# pointer would not show there, so a run of the Mac app with its imports counted is still the proof (linux/PLAN.md,
# step 0). linux/import_census.py checks this file against an image and counts it.
